desc:
A well-formed parentheses string s is given a score by these rules:

  • "()" has score 1.
  • If A and B are well-formed strings, the concatenation AB has score score(A) + score(B).
  • If A is a well-formed string, (A) has score 2 * score(A).

For example "(()(()))" is (A) with A = "()(())", and score(A) = 1 + 2 = 3, so the total score is 6.

Deep nesting makes scores huge, so return the score of s modulo 1,000,000,007.
constraints: s contains only ( and ) and is well-formed
hints: The rules describe a recursion. Which part of the string does each recursive call work on?
Process the string left to right and keep, for every currently open bracket, the total score of what has been completed inside it so far.
On '(' push 0. On ')' pop the inner total v and add max(2 * v, 1) to the new top of the stack: an empty pair () is worth 1, otherwise the inside is doubled.
editorial: Keep a stack of running totals, starting with a single 0 for the top level. Opening a bracket starts a fresh total for its inside by pushing 0. Closing a bracket pops the inside total v; the finished pair contributes 1 if its inside was empty (v = 0) and 2v otherwise, i.e. max(2v, 1). That contribution is added to the total of the enclosing level, which realises the rule AB = A + B.

After the scan the single remaining value is the answer. Take everything modulo 109+7: the true score can be as large as 22499. Since v is reduced modulo p, max(2v, 1) must only treat the genuinely empty inside specially; the inside of a non-empty pair has a true score of at least 1, but its residue can be 0, so track emptiness by whether the bracket was immediately closed, not by the value. Time is O(n), space O(n). A neat O(1)-space alternative adds 2^depth for every "()" found.
